waypoints.name: Frosty Mountain / Lightning Lake Trailhead, E.C. Manning Provincial Park, BC — not a lawful US entry
waypoints.note: Canada-side approach, distinct from the US-side scramble approach: start at the Frosty Mountain trail from Lightning Lake Day Use area in Manning Park, hike toward the Frosty Mountain crest, then head cross-country south over the US border, descending into the Princess Creek basin and traversing to the Princess/Crow Creek divide, then down into Crow Creek to the glacier at the base of Castle Peak's North Face.

waypoints.name: Castle Peak Summit (East Turret - true summit)

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
hazards: At least four unmarked lines on one wall, two of them starting close together on the same buttress
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the climbing
Roughly half the pitches are at the upper end of the grade, with the crux on a corner low down
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger, not by reversing the climb
Multi-day approach and a retreat measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

First, place the central buttress. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is not on it. This route takes the left margin of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

Second, find the gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge. The start is in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

Third, and this is the confirmation higher up that nothing else on the face gives you: this route follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock.

Negative markers, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lightning Lake, E.C. Manning Provincial Park (British Columbia)

approach_variants.notes:
Read the legal point first. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it follows the marked trail from Lightning Lake up the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south over the boundary, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Several unmarked routes on one face, two of them on the same buttress
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger rather than the way you came up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come down toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the left margin of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. The confirmation above is a yellow quartz dyke, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

Negative markers. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

bivy.name: Castle Peak north-side glacier bivy
bivy.notes: Most parties come in from Manning Park, leave the Monument 78 trail near the border and cross a high pass near 8,000 ft to camp below the glacier under the north face.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on rock and moraine; no established sites.

bivy.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Note that a large lightning fire that began in mid July 2026 closed the road above the Monument Creek trailhead along with much of the northern wilderness, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
bivy.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

bivy.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
bivy.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
bivy.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

bivy.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
bivy.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
bivy.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
bivy.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

approach_variants.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.
